newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Lee says Taiwan doesn't fear China's intimidation.
newsitem.headline: Lee says Taiwan doesn't fear China's intimidation.

text.p: President Lee Teng-hui on Thursday accused rival China of attacking Taiwan through an upcoming visit by exiled Tibetan spiritual leader the Dalai Lama, but vowed his island would not be intimidated.

"The Chinese communists have repeatedly used the Dalai Lama's visit to attack us," Lee said in comments issued by the state-funded Central News Agency. "We should not be afraid of the Chinese communists' intimidation."

The Dalai Lama, who has lived in exile in India since the failure of an anti-Chinese uprising in his Himalayan homeland in 1959, was scheduled to arrive in Nationalist-ruled Taiwan on Saturday for a six-day visit.
Despite protests from China, President Lee, a church-going Presbyterian, has expressed a desire to meet the Tibetan Buddhist god-king during his stay in Taiwan.
No such meeting has been announced by Lee's office.
Beijing has repeatedly attacked both Lee and the Dalai Lama as "splittists" who were struggling for the same goal -- independence from China for both Taiwan and Tibet.
Taiwan and China split after a bitter civil war ended in 1949.
The Dalai Lama, who won the 1989 Nobel Peace Prize for his non-violent campaign for autonomy in his Himalayan homeland, has described the Taiwan visit as "strictly spiritual".
Similarly, Taiwan has tried to tone down the political implications of the Dalai Lama's visit by saying he would not engage in official affairs while on the island.
But opposition lawmakers in Taiwan have lashed out at the government, saying it would be disrespectful to the Dalai Lama if he is not treated as a political leader.
China has repeatedly warned Taiwan against admitting the Dalai Lama, saying his trip would harm reunification and ethnic harmony in China.
Beijing vows to attack Taiwan if the island tries to declare independence.
